questions.q: Calculate the percentage composition of carbon in glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) given atomic masses: C = 12.01 u, H = 1.008 u, O = 16.00 u.
questions.a: Correct answer: 40.00%. Molar mass of glucose = 6(12.01) + 12(1.008) + 6(16.00) = 180.156 g/mol. Mass of carbon = 6 × 12.01 = 72.06 g. %C = (72.06/180.156)×100 = 40.00%. A wrong answer like 40% without decimal places reveals the student is rounding atomic masses prematurely (using 12, 1, 16) which gives 40.0% but loses precision needed for empirical formula work. An answer of 33.3% reveals the student divided by number of elements (3) instead of calculating mass contribution.

questions.q: A student calculates %O in H₂SO₄ as (16/98)×100 = 16.33%. Explain why this is incorrect and give the correct calculation.
questions.a: The student used atomic mass of one oxygen atom (16 u) instead of total mass of oxygen in the formula unit. H₂SO₄ has 4 oxygen atoms, so total oxygen mass = 4 × 16.00 = 64.00 g/mol. Molar mass = 2(1.008) + 32.06 + 64.00 = 98.076 g/mol. Correct %O = (64.00/98.076)×100 = 65.26%. This error reveals the student confuses "atomic mass of an element" with "total mass of that element in one formula unit" - a critical distinction for polyatomic compounds.

questions.q: A 5.00 g sample of a compound containing only C, H, and O gives 11.00 g CO₂ and 4.50 g H₂O on complete combustion. Find the percentage composition of each element in the compound.
questions.a:
Step 1: Moles CO₂ = 11.00/44.01 = 0.2499 mol → moles C = 0.2499 mol → mass C = 0.2499 × 12.01 = 3.001 g.
Step 2: Moles H₂O = 4.50/18.015 = 0.2498 mol → moles H = 2 × 0.2498 = 0.4996 mol → mass H = 0.4996 × 1.008 = 0.5036 g.
Step 3: Mass O = 5.00 - 3.001 - 0.5036 = 1.495 g.
Step 4: %C = (3.001/5.00)×100 = 60.02%; %H = (0.5036/5.00)×100 = 10.07%; %O = (1.495/5.00)×100 = 29.91%.
A wrong answer where %C+%H+%O ≠ 100% reveals arithmetic errors or forgetting that oxygen mass is found by difference. Using 44 and 18 instead of 44.01 and 18.015 gives slightly off values (60.0%, 10.0%, 30.0%) - acceptable for board exams but shows rounding awareness.

questions.q: Two samples of a compound are analyzed. Sample A: 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Sample B: 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Both have molar mass 180 g/mol. Are they necessarily the same compound? Explain.
questions.a: Yes, they are the same compound. Identical percentage composition means identical empirical formula (CH₂O, empirical mass = 30 g/mol). With molar mass 180 g/mol, n = 180/30 = 6, giving molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ for both. The Law of Definite Proportions states a given compound always has the same elemental composition by mass. A "no" answer reveals confusion: the student might think different structural isomers (like glucose vs fructose) are "different compounds" in terms of percentage composition - but isomers have identical % composition. This question tests understanding that % composition determines empirical formula, and with molar mass, molecular formula - but not structure.

questions.q: A student claims: "Since NaCl is 39.3% Na and 60.7% Cl, in 100 g of NaCl there are 39.3 g Na atoms and 60.7 g Cl atoms." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is correct in terms of mass but chemically imprecise. "Na atoms" and "Cl atoms" is wrong - in solid NaCl, there are no discrete Na atoms or Cl atoms; there are Na⁺ ions and Cl⁻ ions in a crystal lattice. The masses are correct: 39.3 g of sodium (as Na⁺ ions) and 60.7 g of chlorine (as Cl⁻ ions). A fully correct statement: "In 100 g of NaCl, the mass of sodium is 39.3 g and mass of chlorine is 60.7 g." This evaluates understanding of ionic vs molecular compounds and precision in chemical language - crucial for board exam answer writing.

questions.q: Design a method to check the purity of a commercial sample of washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) using only percentage composition analysis. What %Na would you expect for pure sample?
questions.a: Expected %Na for pure Na₂CO₃·10H₂O: Molar mass = 2(23) + 12 + 3(16) + 10(18) = 286 g/mol. Mass Na = 46 g. %Na = (46/286)×100 = 16.08%. Method: Accurately weigh ~2 g sample, dissolve, precipitate carbonate as CaCO₃ using excess CaCl₂, filter, dry, weigh CaCO₃. From mass CaCO₃, calculate mass CO₃²⁻, then mass Na₂CO₃, then %Na. Compare to 16.08%. Lower %Na indicates impurities (like NaCl, Na₂SO₄) or partial dehydration. A poor answer would suggest "measure %Na directly" without a chemical method, or forget the water of crystallization in molar mass (giving %Na = 46/106 = 43.4% for anhydrous). This tests application to real-world quality control and hydrate handling.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Percentage ______ of a compound is the mass percent of each constituent element present in one mole of the compound, calculated as (total mass of the element in one formula unit / molar mass of the compound) × 100.

Fill in the blank: Observe a packet of common salt (NaCl) in your kitchen - it always tastes the same whether from Gujarat or Tamil Nadu because sodium and ______ combine in a fixed 39.34% Na and 60.66% Cl ratio by mass.
What is Percentage composition of a compound? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Percentage composition of a compound is the mass percent of each constituent element present in one mole of the compound, calculated as (total mass of the element in one formula unit / molar mass of the compound) × 100.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Percentage composition of a compound is the mass percent of each constituent element present in one mole of the compound, calculated as (total mass of the element in one formula unit / molar mass of the compound) × ______.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Percentage composition of a compound?
questions.a: Students calculate percentage composition using atomic numbers instead of atomic masses.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can calculate the percentage composition of any compound given its molecular formula and atomic masses, and can use percentage composition data to verify sample purity or determine empirical formulas.
